name: zlib-ng
workload: Compress and decompress silesia.tar (212 MB) single thread via lzbench; zlib-ng 2.3.3 vs zlib 1.3.2 at levels 1, 6, 9.
claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4 level 6: compress 62.1 MB/s vs zlib 26.8 MB/s (2.3x, derived from page data), decompress 498 MB/s vs 314 MB/s (1.6x, derived from page data); ratio 32.51% vs 32.19%. Level 1: 196 vs 89.0 MB/s compress but ratio 44.41% vs 36.45%. README: x86-64 can be about 4x faster than stock zlib.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench 2.4 release binary lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15); compiler flags not listed in README; options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04
tradeoffs: Drop-in zlib API in compat mode; output differs from zlib at the same level (slightly lower ratio at level 1 and at level 6); uses CPU intrinsics with runtime dispatch.
caveats: Single-thread lzbench numbers are from a third-party suite whose README does not list compiler flags. A separate zlib-ng discussion (benchmark_url alternative https://github.com/zlib-ng/zlib-ng/discussions/871) shows ~4x faster level-9 compress and 2.5x faster decompress on an i9-9900K with GCC 4.8.5 (2021, maintainer-run). libdeflate is faster than zlib-ng on whole-buffer work but has no streaming.
found_via: WebSearch: 'zlib-ng benchmark faster than zlib deflate inflate compression library github'; lzbench README table

name: ZXC
workload: Decompression speed on silesia.tar (single thread) vs LZ4, LZ4HC and zstd, via lzbench.
claimed_speedup: README: 22-75% faster decode than LZ4 at the default level at equal or better ratio; decode vs LZ4 1.36x on EPYC 9B45 and 1.75x on Apple M2, vs zstd 2.21x on EPYC 9B45 and 2.60x on Apple M2. lzbench 2.4 (EPYC 9555P): zxc 0.14.1 -3 decompress 4716 MB/s at ratio 46.09% vs lz4 1.10.0 3832 MB/s at 47.60%; zxc -1 8151 MB/s at 61.76%.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench 2.4 release binary lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15); compiler flags not listed in README; options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4; project README: lzbench 2.3.1 with MOREFLAGS=-march=native, Clang 21 (macOS) and GCC 14 (Linux)
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04; README also Apple M2, Axion Neoverse-V2, EPYC 9B45 (Zen 5), EPYC 7B13 (Zen 3)
tradeoffs: Asymmetric codec: decode-optimised, compression much slower than LZ4 at the same ratio (zxc -3 compresses at 168 MB/s vs lz4 550 MB/s). Bindings for Rust, Python, Node.js, Go, WASM; optional seekable archives.
caveats: Win is decompression only; compress speed is lower than LZ4 at comparable ratios. Young project (format version 0.x). The lzbench rows were read from the lzbench README; the project's own table was read from its README.
found_via: WebSearch: 'C++ compression library faster than zstd lz4 benchmark github lzbench'

name: LZAV
workload: In-memory compress and decompress of silesia.tar vs LZ4 and Snappy.
claimed_speedup: README (Apple M1): LZAV 5.18 compress 627 MB/s, decompress 3830 MB/s, ratio 39.91% vs Snappy 1.1.10 495 / 3230 MB/s, 48.22%; vs LZ4 1.9.4 700 / 4570 MB/s, 47.60%. lzbench 2.4 (EPYC 9555P): lzav 5.17 -1 compress 451 MB/s, decompress 2527 MB/s, 39.91% vs snappy 1.3.1 457 / 976 MB/s, 47.85%.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench 2.4 release binary lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15); compiler flags not listed in README; options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4; README: Apple clang 15.0.0 arm64 macOS; LLVM clang 19.1.7 x86-64 AlmaLinux 9.6
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04; README: Apple M1 3.5 GHz, Xeon E-2386G 5.1 GHz
tradeoffs: Decompressor needs the original length stored separately; blocks up to 2 GiB; ~16% better ratio than LZ4 at lower compress speed.
caveats: Not faster than LZ4: LZ4 compresses and decompresses faster in both README and lzbench. The win over Snappy is decompression (2.6x in lzbench, derived from page data) and ratio; compression is on par with Snappy in lzbench (451 vs 457 MB/s). Baseline Snappy is outside the list; LZ4 comparison is a ratio-only win.
found_via: WebSearch: 'C++ compression library faster than zstd lz4 benchmark github lzbench'

name: misa77
workload: Decompression speed on silesia.tar, single thread, via lzbench.
claimed_speedup: README (Intel i7-14650HX, turbo off): level 1 decompress 5376 MB/s at 42.64% vs LZ4 1.10.0 2514 MB/s at 47.59% (2.1x); vs zstd 1.5.7 -1 903 MB/s at 34.54%. lzbench 2.4 (EPYC 9555P): misa77 0.6.0 -1 decompress 7813 MB/s at 42.65% vs lz4 1.10.0 3832 MB/s at 47.60%; compress 73.8 MB/s vs lz4 550 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench 2.4 release binary lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15); compiler flags not listed in README; options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04; README: Intel Core i7-14650HX 2.2 GHz and Apple M3
tradeoffs: Needs C++20, little-endian 64-bit only; compression much slower than LZ4 (about 7x slower at level 1 in lzbench); unsafe decoder faster than safe mode by ~5%; level 4 has no safe decoder yet.
caveats: Format may change unexpectedly (v0.x.y). Ratio at level 1 (42.65%) is worse than zstd -1 (34.53%), so the win is a decode-throughput vs ratio trade-off against LZ4, not against zstd on ratio.
found_via: lzbench README results table (surfaced while verifying lzbench rows)

name: Kanzi (kanzi-cpp)
workload: Compress and decompress silesia.tar vs xz, zstd, brotli, bzip2, gzip at matched ratios.
claimed_speedup: README (Ryzen 9 9950X, multithreaded): kanzi -l 7 compress 1150 ms / decompress 885 ms at 47,330,431 B vs xz 5.8.1 -9 43611 ms / 931 ms at 48,802,580 B (38x faster compress, derived from page data). lzbench 2.4 single thread (EPYC 9555P): kanzi 2.5.3 -7 10.8 MB/s compress at ratio 22.32% vs xz 5.8.4 -9 2.75 MB/s at 23.01% (3.9x, derived from page data); decompress 15.8 vs 122 MB/s (slower).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench 2.4 release binary lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15); compiler flags not listed in README; options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04; README: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X 16-core, Ubuntu 26.04.1
tradeoffs: Context-modelling / BWT pipeline: much slower decompression than xz in single-thread lzbench (kanzi -7 15.8 vs xz 122 MB/s); multithreaded in its own CLI; high memory use at top levels.
caveats: The README comparison uses kanzi with threads versus single-thread xz, so the large README speedup is partly parallelism; the single-thread lzbench figures are the fair ones. At low levels kanzi is roughly on par with zstd, not clearly faster.
found_via: WebSearch: 'bzip3 OR fast-lzma2 OR kanzi OR openzl compression faster than xz zstd benchmark github'

name: bzip3
workload: Compress silesia.tar single thread via lzbench; project README compares bzip2, xz, zstd on Perl5 release tarballs.
claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4 (EPYC 9555P): bzip3 1.5.4 -5 compress 11.9 MB/s at ratio 22.29% vs xz 5.8.4 -9 2.75 MB/s at 23.01% (4.3x faster compress, derived from page data); decompress 12.4 vs 122 MB/s (slower). README (Perl5 tarballs): bzip3 -b 256 decompress 4m06s vs bzip2 -9 9m22s, xz -9 4m40s, zstd -16 3m51s with smaller output than all three.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench 2.4 release binary lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15); compiler flags not listed in README; options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04
tradeoffs: BWT plus context mixing; strongest on text and source; decompression is about 10x slower than xz in single-thread lzbench. Bundled libsais and LZP parts are Apache-2.0; core is LGPL.
caveats: Claim is compress-time and ratio versus xz and bzip2 (bzip2 is outside the list); not a decompression win versus xz. README numbers were run on an HDD with compiler-dependent speed and no stated CPU model.
found_via: WebSearch: 'bzip3 OR fast-lzma2 OR kanzi OR openzl compression faster than xz zstd benchmark github'

name: Fast LZMA2 (fast-lzma2)
workload: LZMA2 compression of silesia.tar vs reference LZMA2 (7-Zip 19.00 in the README; xz and LZMA SDK in lzbench).
claimed_speedup: README: 20% to 100% speed gain at the higher levels over the default LZMA2 in 7-Zip, with a small ratio loss (two threads, Silesia). lzbench 2.4 single thread (EPYC 9555P): fastlzma2 1.0.1 -8 compress 4.52 MB/s at ratio 23.18% vs xz 5.8.4 -9 2.75 MB/s at 23.01% (1.6x, derived from page data); -10 3.38 MB/s at 22.96% vs lzma 26.03 -9 2.55 MB/s at 22.97%.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench 2.4 release binary lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15); compiler flags not listed in README; options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04
tradeoffs: Needs about twice the dictionary size in memory to reach the ratio of LZMA2; output 1%-5% larger than 7-Zip's at default; decompression speed is the same as LZMA2 (~79 MB/s in lzbench).
caveats: Compression-only speedup; xz decompression is not improved. Baseline in the README is 7-Zip LZMA2 (same algorithm as xz) rather than xz itself. Dual license recorded as in the README (BSD-3-Clause and GPL-2.0).
found_via: WebSearch: 'bzip3 OR fast-lzma2 OR kanzi OR openzl compression faster than xz zstd benchmark github'

name: OpenZL
workload: Format-aware compression of structured datasets (trained compressors) vs zstd and xz; separate native LZ engine vs zstd on Silesia.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (search result summaries of the Meta blog, arXiv 2510.03203 and Phoronix, not opened): a trained OpenZL compressor compresses at 340 MB/s vs zstd -3 at 220 MB/s and xz -9 at 3.5 MB/s with a better ratio; ppmf_person compresses 55% better than xz -9 and 11x as fast; OpenZL 0.3 native LZ engine decompresses Silesia at 3,062 MB/s vs 1,254 MB/s for zstd (reported as 144% faster).
tradeoffs: Wins come from describing the data format and training a compressor graph; decompression of format-aware streams is slower than zstd; API and format subject to change off release tags; requires C11 and C++17.
caveats: Numbers are from blocked pages seen only as search snippets; the repo README and benchmark/ README give no results. Gains apply to structured data, not arbitrary byte streams. The repo is a benchmark target in lzbench (openzl 0.2.3) but the lzbench README results table has no openzl rows.
found_via: WebSearch: 'OpenZL format-aware compression speedup compared to zstd xz compression ratio decompression speed results'

name: zlib-rs
workload: Level-9 compression and decompression of Silesia-small.tar via deflatebench/minigzip, single file mode.
claimed_speedup: zlib-ng discussion 871, run by mxmlnkn on 2025-08-05: level-9 compress zlib-rs 0.493 s vs zlib 2.106 s (4.3x, derived from page data) at ratio 40.409% vs 40.490%; page notes decompression is about 3x faster than zlib for the optimised variants. README: performance generally on par with zlib-ng.
stars_or_usage: 698 stars; recommended by Cloudflare as successor to its zlib fork
tradeoffs: Rust crate with a C-compatible shared library; memory-safe; needs a Rust toolchain to build from source.
caveats: Rust implementation, usable from C++ through the C ABI. Independent run lives on a zlib-ng page. Search snippets also report zlib-rs 6-10%+ faster than zlib-ng at decompression for 1 KB to 65 KB chunks (Trifecta blog, blocked, snippet only); some users saw parity.
found_via: WebSearch: 'zlib-rs faster than zlib-ng decompression inflate benchmark percent github trifectatechfoundation'

name: ISA-L (igzip)
workload: Compress silesia.tar with igzip levels 0-3 vs zlib and libdeflate via TurboBench.
claimed_speedup: zlib-ng issue 1486 (powturbo, 2023-05-10): igzip level 2 compress 598.69 MB/s at ratio 36.1% vs zlib level 9 27.79 MB/s at 32.2% (the page's zlib level-1/6 rows were not seen; ratio is not matched). Decompress for igzip not seen in the quoted rows.

name: Wuffs deflate/zlib/gzip decoder
workload: Deflate, gzip and zlib decode of 1k, 10k and 100k inputs vs zlib via 'mimic' wrapper.
claimed_speedup: README: decodes deflate up to 1.4x faster than zlib-the-library (C). doc/benchmarks.md (Sept 2022, v0.3.0-rc.1, i5-10210U, clang 11): deflate decode 100k 521 MB/s vs zlib 352 MB/s (1.48x), 10k 409 vs 289 MB/s (1.41x), 1k 195 vs 241 MB/s (0.81x); gzip 100k 1.81x; zlib 100k 1.56x.
compiler_and_flags: clang/llvm 11.0.1 and gcc 10.2.1; flags not stated
stars_or_usage: 4.8k stars; GIF decoder ships in Chrome
tradeoffs: Memory-safe language; generated C is distributed as a single file usable from C and C++; decode only for deflate (no compression).
caveats: Numbers from 2022 and first-party; small 1 KB inputs are slower than zlib; the doc also lists libdeflate and miniz, and libdeflate is typically faster still. Language is Wuffs, consumed as generated C.
found_via: WebSearch: 'zlib-ng benchmark...' follow-up; github.com/google/wuffs README and doc/benchmarks.md

name: libslz (SLZ)
workload: Compress silesia.tar to gzip single thread (lzbench) and README per-file runs.
claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4 (EPYC 9555P): slz_gzip 1.3.1 -1 compress 316 MB/s at ratio 46.97% vs zlib 1.3.2 -1 89.0 MB/s at 36.45% (3.6x, derived from page data). README (Core i5-3320M, Silesia): SLZ 232-293 MB/s vs zlib 70-88 MB/s, about 3x, with 24-32% larger output, ~90% less memory per stream.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench 2.4 release binary lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15); compiler flags not listed in README; options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04; README: Intel Core i5-3320M 3.3 GHz
tradeoffs: Stateless, no history window beyond a few bytes; much worse ratio than zlib; compression only (output is plain gzip/deflate/zlib readable by any inflater); 28 bytes per stream.
caveats: Speedup is bought with a 24-32% size penalty so it competes with zlib level 1 and LZ4-class use. X11 license is MIT-style.
